title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
purpose: It compiles, from Ismaili legal and esoteric sources, the etiquette of the privy and the ablution, the rulings on valid and invalid purifying water, and the enumerated obligatory and Sunnah acts of wudhu, ghusl and disliked places of prayer, closing with the inner (batini) interpretation of ablution as purification by knowledge.

points.text: The book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daaim al-Islam rules that one who prayed while a known impurity was upon him — having forgotten the istinja — must repeat the prayer, since prayer is not permitted while a man carries an impurity of which he knows until he washes it away.

The same source distinguishes obligation from excellence: the Imams' concealment of themselves in water was mentioned for the excellence of good manners, so a man who uncovers himself where no one sees him commits no harm and prays validly with that purity, though concealment is better.

Tawil al-Shariah lists twelve manners of the wudhu governing the privy — entering with sandals, advancing the left foot, covering the head, not facing or turning the back to the qiblah, concealing oneself, leaning on the left leg, not sitting long, not cleansing with human excrement or worn bone or animal droppings but with three fresh stones, cleansing with the left hand, not pouring water on excrement, not speaking, and advancing the right foot on leaving.

The section holds, on the authority of the Prophet, that prayer is not valid or accepted without ablution and purification, and reports his forbidding urination in burrows because they are the lairs of serpents and snakes.

Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Manners is cited for rinsing the mouth and drawing water into the nose as Sunnah purification, istinja with cold water cutting off piles, ablution after purification earning ten good deeds, the formula 'In the name of God — make me among those who repent and purify themselves' said before touching water, concealing oneself because Satan covets the uncovered man, not baring the thigh before a company, and washing children's hands of food-grease lest Satan smell it and harm the two recording angels.

A key distinction is drawn between acts that are Sunnah and acts that are obligatory for another reason: rinsing the mouth, drawing in water and istinja are Sunnah practices not to be deliberately abandoned, and omitting them does not spoil the prayer — yet the istinja remains obligatory insofar as the removal of impurity is itself obligatory.

Rulings of accommodation are given for the injured and incapacitated: one with a wound or boil that water cannot touch wipes over the bandages, and performs tayammum if removal would harm him through cold or severe injury or if he is sick; in the greater purification he pours water in a stream, and performs tayammum if he fears for himself, whether traveling or at home; and a man whose hands are cut off has the wudhu performed for him by his bondmaid or wife, failing which he performs tayammum and prays.

On water, the answers hold that water above the Shariah-stated measure which overpowers impurity remains valid for purification, whereas water in a vessel in which an impurity has become apparent becomes impure and is not made valid by pouring more water in a stream unless it rises above the measure after the vessel is purified; a pool eight cubits in length and breadth, even a span deep, is valid; rainwater running with filth into a great pool is valid so long as color, taste and smell are unchanged; and used water and used dust may be used for purification once and many times.

The saying 'Whoever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' is interpreted esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and likewise the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, nothing else will purify him.

Majalis al-Bayan enumerates the seven obligations of wudhu (pure water, intention, washing face, washing hands, wiping head, wiping feet, and the order in which God mentioned them), its twelve Sunnah acts, the seven obligatory forms of ghusl (including washing the dead as a collective obligation on the living), the twelve Sunnah forms of ghusl, and the twelve places where prayer is disliked.

Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl in al-Risalah al-Maknunah divides purity and filth into two kinds: outward purity is achieved by outward water, cleansing the outward filth of urine and excrement, while inward purity is achieved by inward water — which is knowledge — cleansing the inward filth of doubt and ignorance.

The same author reads the seven acts of wudhu as seven bounds — three Sunnah (rinsing the mouth, drawing in water, istinja), two washings and two wipings, one of each bounded and one unbounded — and interprets the mouth as the sole conveyor of nourishment to the senses, the nostrils as the breath by which the body lives, and the face, with its seven openings, as bearing the meaning of the Speaker, since as a person is known by his face so no one is known except through his prophet and there is no deliverance except by turning toward him.

The section closes with Ali's ruling that there is no dissimulation (taqiyyah) permitted in the drinking of intoxicants or in wiping over the socks, consistent with Tawil al-Shariah's report that the Prophet forbade wiping over the socks and forbade abandoning the audible saying of the basmalah.
